title: Act III, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Brutus speaks to the plebeians in prose: he loved Caesar, but loved Rome more; Caesar was ambitious, so he killed him. The crowd cheers and even shouts to make Brutus Caesar. Brutus leaves Antony to speak. Antony, in verse, repeats that 'Brutus is an honourable man' until the phrase turns to irony; recalls Caesar refusing the crown; weeps; shows the torn, bloody mantle; and finally reads Caesar's will, which leaves every citizen seventy-five drachmas and his private gardens. The crowd riots to burn the conspirators' houses. Antony hears Octavius is in Rome and that Brutus and Cassius have fled.

context.history: Roman funeral orations (laudationes) praised the dead in public. Rhetoric, the study of persuasion, was central to Roman and Elizabethan education; students practiced ethos, pathos and logos.

significance: This is the play's great study in persuasion. Brutus appeals to reason and his own honor; Antony uses repetition, irony, props, delay and emotion. The crowd's swing shows how rhetoric can move a republic toward violence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its theme shape the reader's understanding of the funeral orations. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene II suggests about the funeral orations. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's theme and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses theme in Act III, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of the funeral orations. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the funeral orations responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the funeral orations follows or bends those conventions, using the theme as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene II and its treatment of the funeral orations. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's theme and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about the funeral orations in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the funeral orations. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

literaryElements.label: Rhetoric
literaryElements.explanation: Brutus's speech is in prose, logical and restrained ("Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more"); Antony's is verse, emotional, ironic and dramatic, with the will and the body as props.

literaryElements.label: Irony
literaryElements.explanation: Antony's repeated "Brutus is an honourable man" turns praise into accusation.

literaryElements.label: Structure
literaryElements.explanation: The crowd's lines show their shifts in real time.

themesAndDevelopment.development: the scene is a masterclass in ethos, pathos and logos.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: honour
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: "Honourable" is a key word; Antony turns it into irony in the funeral oration. In this scene: “be silent, that you may hear: believe me for mine honour, and have respect to mine honour, that you may believe: censure” (Act III, Scene II, Brutus (speech 6)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: be silent, that you may hear: believe me for mine honour, and have respect to mine honour, that you may believe: censure

symbolsAndMotifs.name: blood
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Blood turns the assassination from sacrifice into butchery; the conspirators bathe their hands in it. In this scene: “dead Caesar’s wounds / And dip their napkins in his sacred blood, / Yea, beg a hair of him for memory, / And, dying, mention” (Act III, Scene II, Antony (speech 39)).

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
